title: Query-Efficient Hard-label Black-box Attack: An Optimization-based Approach (OPT)
authors: Minhao Cheng, Thong Le, Pin-Yu Chen, Jinfeng Yi, Huan Zhang, Cho-Jui Hsieh

pages.title: Turning a label oracle into an optimization problem
pages.subtitle: The OPT attack in one sentence

blocks.html: The Boundary Attack proved that label-only attacks are possible, but it explored the boundary with a random walk and paid for it with enormous query counts. This paper reframes the hard-label attack as a well-defined continuous optimization problem, so that classic zeroth-order optimization can drive the search far more efficiently.

pages.title: The hard-label setting, recapped
pages.subtitle: Why the usual objective fails here

blocks.html: Recall the hard-label / decision-based threat model: the attacker submits inputs and sees only the final predicted label — no probabilities, no logits, no gradients. Success is measured by queries-to-success, i.e. how many model evaluations are needed to reach a small perturbation norm.

The reason standard attacks break is that the natural loss function is a step function of the input: as you move an image, the predicted label stays constant and then suddenly jumps. A step function has zero gradient almost everywhere and is undefined at the jump, so you cannot optimize it directly, and you cannot even estimate its gradient by finite differences — tiny probes return the same label and look like zero change.

The whole trick of this paper is to replace that discontinuous label loss with a smooth, real-valued quantity that the label oracle can measure: the distance to the decision boundary along a chosen direction.

pages.title: Optimize the direction, measure the distance
pages.subtitle: From input space to direction space

blocks.html: Instead of asking "which pixels should I perturb?", OPT asks "in which direction from the original image is the boundary closest?". For any unit direction $\theta$, define $g(\theta)$ as the distance you must travel from the original image $x_0$ along $\theta$ before the prediction changes. That distance is exactly the radius at which $\theta$ first becomes adversarial.

In words: walk outward from $x_0$ in direction $\theta$ and record the first distance $\lambda$ at which the hard-label classifier $f$ changes its answer. Small $g(\theta)$ means the boundary is near in that direction — a good place to plant a small perturbation.

The attack reduces to this clean objective: find the direction whose boundary distance is smallest. The optimal $\theta^{*}$ gives the smallest adversarial perturbation, of size $g(\theta^{*})$. Unlike the raw label loss, $g(\theta)$ is continuous in $\theta$, so it can actually be optimized.

Computing $g(\theta)$ needs only hard labels. First do a coarse search outward until the label flips, bracketing the boundary. Then binary search between the last adversarial and last non-adversarial radii to pin down the crossing distance to any desired precision. Each query answers one yes/no question, and binary search converts that into a real number with only logarithmically many queries.

items: Coarse step: increase $\lambda$ until the predicted label changes, giving a bracket.
Binary search: halve the bracket repeatedly until $g(\theta)$ is known to the target tolerance.
Result: a smooth value extracted from a discontinuous oracle, at a cost of a handful of queries per evaluation.

pages.title: Zeroth-order optimization of the direction
pages.subtitle: Estimating the gradient of g without gradients

blocks.html: We can evaluate $g(\theta)$ but we have no analytic gradient for it. So OPT uses a zeroth-order (gradient-free) estimate: perturb the direction by a random vector $u$, measure how $g$ changes, and use that finite difference as a stand-in for the directional derivative.

Read it as: probe the boundary in a slightly rotated direction $\theta + \beta u$, see whether the boundary got nearer or farther, and turn that difference into an estimated gradient pointing toward closer boundaries. Averaging several random $u$ reduces noise. Then take a standard gradient-descent step on $\theta$ and renormalize.
Each gradient estimate is expensive here: every $g$ evaluation hides a whole binary search, and we need several per step. This is exactly the cost that Sign-OPT later attacks.

pages.title: Far fewer queries than the random walk
pages.subtitle: OPT versus Boundary Attack

blocks.html: By turning exploration into directed optimization, OPT reaches the same perturbation sizes as the Boundary Attack using 3–4× fewer queries, and it converges in cases where the random walk stalls. It also handles both untargeted and targeted attacks (the latter by walking toward a target-class image), and applies beyond images, for example to discrete or otherwise non-differentiable models, because it only ever needs the label oracle.

The provable-convergence framing was itself a contribution: because $g(\theta)$ is a genuine continuous objective, the attack inherits convergence guarantees from zeroth-order optimization theory, unlike the heuristic random walk.

pages.title: Why this paper mattered
pages.subtitle: The reformulation everything else builds on

blocks.html: OPT's lasting contribution is the direction-and-distance formulation: $\min_{\theta} g(\theta)$, with $g$ measured by binary search. This single idea makes the hard-label problem differentiable-in-spirit and opens it to the full toolbox of zeroth-order optimization.

Its remaining bottleneck is the price of each gradient estimate: every evaluation of $g$ is a binary search, and a gradient needs many of them. Sign-OPT removes most of that cost by noticing you only need the sign of the directional derivative, not its magnitude.
OPT: reformulate the attack as minimizing the distance-to-boundary $g(\theta)$ along a direction, estimate that distance by binary search, and optimize $\theta$ with zeroth-order gradients.
